title: B4 follow-on: cementing double-key distractors and one duplicate

items.flag: options 1 and 2 both algebraically equal to the correct formula
items.reason: Both distractors were the same ratio rewritten; replaced with the post-sag standoff and the washout case, both wrong for the reported number.

1.old: The blade less the casing, over twice the clearance between the casing and the bore.
1.new: The standoff at mid-span, after the sag between two centralizers is subtracted.

2.old: The ratio of the two annular gaps, blade to casing and bore to casing.
2.new: The blade ratio worked on the effective bore of a washed-out hole.

items.reason: Option 2 restated the sag-only ceiling; now uses the deflection term, which the ceiling excludes. Option 1 lengthened slightly to keep a 6-character gap to the key.

2.old: One less the sag over the clearance, which caps what any spring can achieve at that spacing.
2.new: One less the spring deflection over the clearance, which caps what any spacing can achieve.

1.old: The standoff a rigid centralizer with a blade equal to the bore would reach, which is the theoretical maximum for the geometry.
1.new: The standoff a rigid centralizer with a blade equal to the bore would reach, which is the theoretical maximum for the geometry of the hole.

items.flag: option 2 nearly restates the correct option
items.reason: Option 2 restated the lesson's reasons; now claims booleans cannot be weighted, which the lesson shows other software doing.

2.old: Because the weights are unmeasured, a score hides which item failed, and no log gives one.
2.new: Because the five items are booleans, and a boolean cannot be weighted into a percentage.

items.flag: option 2 (float collar depth difference times bore capacity) is the correct explanation
items.reason: Option 2 was the key reworded; now uses the shoe depths and the annular capacity, the wrong capacity for displacement.

2.old: Their float collars are at different depths, times the casing bore capacity.
2.new: Their casing shoes are 200 m apart, times the annular capacity of the open hole.

items.reason: Both were true statements; option 2 now claims the survey converts rows to vertical height, option 3 claims a deviated hole needs less cement at the same measured depth, both contradicted by the lesson.

2.old: The true vertical depth has to be computed separately for the hydrostatic head.
2.new: The survey is used to convert each annulus row to its vertical height first.

3.old: A deviated well needs more cement than a vertical one to the same true vertical depth.
3.new: A deviated well needs less cement than a vertical one of the same measured depth.

items.reason: Option 2 paraphrased the lesson's two-levers point; now claims the engine answer is an upper bound, the reverse of the lesson and the explanation.

2.old: Because it is one of the two biggest levers, and the model can only quantify the other one.
2.new: Because without it the engine's answer is an upper bound on what a good job achieves.

items.flag: option 2 answers the same as the correct option
items.reason: Option 2 gave the same answer (one); now counts the top of cement as a guess, which the lesson treats as a design decision. Option 1 lengthened to keep a 6-character gap to the key.

2.old: One, the open hole excess, and every other input is either a measurement or a design choice.
2.new: Two, the open hole excess and the top of cement, because neither can be measured before the job.

1.old: Two, the excess and the slurry yield, since the yield is measured on a laboratory blend rather than on the field mix.
1.new: Two, the excess and the slurry yield, since the yield is measured on a laboratory blend rather than on the actual field mix.

items.reason: The lesson gives option 2's reason as part of the geometric reason; now claims the casing above needs strong tail to carry its weight, where the lesson calls the lead a filler there.

2.old: Because it is the deepest point protected by the casing above, so strong cement goes in open hole.
2.new: Because the casing string above that depth needs the strong tail behind it to carry its weight.

items.reason: Option 2 restated the key and option 1 was also defensible; option 2 now says nothing changes until the plug bumps, option 1 points at the constant denominator, neither of which explains the flat stretch.

2.old: Because nothing above that shoe changes until cement or spacer crosses it going up.
2.new: Because the annulus sees no change at all until the top plug bumps at the end.

1.old: Because the friction above the shoe is constant at a constant rate, and the head there is fixed by the mud density.
1.new: Because it is divided by the true vertical depth of the previous shoe, which stays the same all through the job.

items.reason: Option 2 restated the key; now claims cement stays inside the casing, whereas the lesson has it in the annulus below the previous shoe by then.

2.old: Because the annulus above that shoe holds only mud until cement or spacer crosses it.
2.new: Because the whole cement column stays inside the casing until the last third of the job.

items.reason: Option 2 restated the key; now includes friction, which is the end pump pressure relation.

2.old: The annulus head less the inside head at the last step, with the friction term excluded.
2.new: The annulus head plus friction less the inside head, at the step where the plug bumps.

items.reason: Option 2 gave the same four steps in the same order; now puts the rate window before the fluid programme that sets it.

2.old: The top of cement, then the fluid programme, then the rate window, and the rate last.
2.new: The top of cement, then the rate window, then a fluid programme to fit inside it.

items.reason: Option 2 gave the same order; now swaps the density profile and the rate window.

2.old: The top of cement, then the fluid programme, then the rate window, and the rate last.
2.new: The top of cement, then the rate window, then the density profile, and the rate last.

items.reason: Option 2 was a true statement from the lesson about the rest; now names a free-fall deficit, which the slant well never has.

2.old: Friction at the last step, which is why the bump falls when the final rate is reduced.
2.new: The free-fall deficit at the last step, which the pumps have to make up at the bump.

items.reason: Option 2 restated the key; now claims the heads are unknown, but the densities are known and only the rate is lost.

2.old: The rate is unknown, and so is all computed from it, so that stretch has no numbers.
2.new: The hydrostatic heads, because the fluid densities cannot be tracked while it falls.

items.flag: near duplicate of intermediate module m03-the-job-over-time ord 9 (same ECD at the casing shoe question, same key)
items.reason: True duplicate; kept the module question and rewrote the final copy to test the null previous-shoe ECD case from the same lesson (ECD at the shoe).

prompt.old: The horizontal well's ECD at the CASING shoe is 1837.9218199066345 kg/m3 before anything is pumped. Why?
prompt.new: When is the ECD at the previous shoe reported as null for the whole run?

0.old: Its mud is heavier than the slant well's.
0.new: When no fracture limit is supplied as an input.

1.old: It divides the friction of a 1600 m lateral by 1214.859173174059 m of true vertical depth.
1.new: When no cased section sits above the casing shoe, as on a conductor or a surface string.

2.old: Its annulus is narrower, so the same rate gives a higher velocity and more friction.
2.new: When cement never reaches the previous shoe, so the annulus there holds only mud.

3.old: Its previous shoe is shallower, so its head gives a higher equivalent density.
3.new: When the previous shoe is shallower than the top of cement on the well.

explanation.old: The friction is generated along the hole and the depth is measured vertically.
explanation.new: With no cased section above the casing shoe there is no shallower shoe to protect, so the peak ECD at the previous shoe is null as well.

items.correct_change_reason: Duplicate rewritten into a new question; the key is the new question's answer at the same index.
